title: Savata the gardener: work as worship
hookLine: a gardener near Pandharpur sings that his onions, radishes and greens are all his god
carry: svakarma: your own work, offered, is worship
tomorrow: where does Krishna say he can be found?

cards: Near Pandharpur, in Maharashtra, the town of the god Vitthala, there lived a gardener named Savata. People still call him Savata Mali, Savata the gardener.
Every year crowds of pilgrims walk past fields like his, singing, on their way to the temple. In the stories told about him, Savata stays in his field. Weeding.
Watering. Pulling onions. And he sings one of the plainest songs any saint ever sang.

teach.b: Savata belongs to the Varkaris, the singing saints of Maharashtra, in the time of Jnaneshwar and Namdev, some seven hundred years ago. His best-loved line is about vegetables.
In paraphrase: onion, radish, greens, all of it is my Vitthala. Not a picture of God beside the vegetables. The vegetables.
The stories say that when he wouldn't leave his work for the temple, the god came out to the field instead. The teaching behind the song is as old as the Gita.

teach.h: GITA 18: WORSHIP WITH YOUR OWN WORK.
teach.b: In its last chapter, Krishna says, in paraphrase: the one from whom all beings come, who pervades all this, worship him with your own work, and you reach perfection. Svakarma: your own work, offered.
Earlier, in chapter thirteen, the Gita describes that same reality with an image for this week of hands: its hands and feet are everywhere.
And the very next verse adds that it has no senses of its own, and holds up everything while clinging to none. Hands everywhere, and bound to none.
So this is the widest mudra. A hand shaped before a shrine means something on purpose. A hand pulling an onion, slicing bread or counting change can mean the same thing, if it's offered.

That's why a cook may offer the first portion before anyone eats, why people honor their tools at Ayudha Puja, why a shop may open with a small prayer at the counter. The tradition doesn't say a job is worship by itself.
It says your own work, done well and offered, already is.

how: Many Hindus offer their daily work as worship: a cook offers the first portion before anyone eats, tools are honored at Ayudha Puja, and devotees recall the Gita's teaching (18.46) that one worships God through one's own work, and the Varkari saints who sang it, such as Savata Mali.

o: a hand pose that keeps work apart from worship
hand shapes allowed only before a temple shrine
shaped hands that carry meaning, widened to every working hand

games.q: work as worship — tap the pairs.

s: Savata Mali sang that his vegetables were his Vitthala
onion, radish, greens: all of it, his god.
the Gita says worship happens only in rituals
in chapter 18 Krishna says to worship him with your own work.
in Gita 13, what is to be known has hands and feet everywhere
and the next verse says it has no senses of its own, and holds up all things, clinging to none.

games.q: you have a dull shift to finish before evening aarti. by the Gita and Savata, what fits?
o: do it well and offer it; your own work is worship too.
rush it; only the aarti counts.
skip the aarti; work is all that matters now.
games.why: Gita 18: worship him with your own work. Savata sang that his vegetables were his god, and he never stopped loving Vitthala.

practice: Rest the hands on the thighs, palms up, and look at them: the lines, the knuckles, the places that do the work.
Close the eyes and let other hands from your day come and go, the ones that grew and cooked your food, the ones that built your chair. Then think of one task waiting for you today.
If you pray, offer it silently before you start: this is for you. If not, decide to do it well, for someone.

wordCard.voice: The mudras. Today, the widest: hands and feet everywhere, and a gardener's hands that made their work a prayer.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: svakarma, one's own work. Gita 18.46 says to worship God with it.
